terms.gloss: indicative; as a noun (modus understood), the indicative
evidence: Diom. p. 329; Prisc. p. 819 P. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The later grammarians’ term, and every grammar’s since: modō indicātīvō, in the indicative mood (Traupman 247). Varro and Quintilian call it fatendī modus, “the mood of stating” (see below).

evidence: Quint. 1.6.7: quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur
terms.comment: Varro’s and Quintilian’s name: the mood in which one declares or owns a thing (fatērī). The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

phrases.latin: omnia, quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur, eadem, sī īnfīnītīs e litteram mediā syllabā accēpērunt, utique prōductam habent
phrases.english: all verbs that end in e and o in the indicative have that e long, if they keep it in the middle syllable of the infinitive

sources: Lewis & Short: fateor · Lewis & Short: indicativus
